teaser: A village funeral painted at the size reserved for kings, and Paris could not forgive it.
review_notes:
Dimensions 315 x 668 cm.
Claim that the scene recalls the burial of Courbet's great-uncle Claude-Etienne Teste in September 1848, in the new Ornans cemetery opened that year: the usual identification, worth a check.
The 1849 medal for After Dinner at Ornans exempting him from the Salon jury: standard account.
The two men in knee breeches as veterans of the 1793 Revolution: traditional identification.
Courbet's remark that the Burial was 'the burial of Romanticism' is paraphrased from a statement he made in the early 1860s; check wording.
Given to the French state by his sister Juliette in 1881; at the Orsay since 1986.
The skull is small in this image (about x 0.585, y 0.94): check the find is fair on a phone.

lesson.text: This canvas was made for one wall: the wall of the Paris Salon, the huge official exhibition where careers were decided. On that wall, a painting almost seven meters wide meant one thing. It showed a coronation, a battle, a scene from the Bible or from Greek myth. Size was a rank, and the top rank belonged to heroes.

In the winter of 1850, visitors found a picture of that rank, 3.15 by 6.68 meters (about 10 by 22 feet), showing a funeral in a small town near the Swiss border. No hero, no saint. Just the people of Ornans, life-size, in their Sunday black, standing around a hole.
Courbet painted it in Ornans, in an attic studio so cramped that he could not step back to see the whole canvas. He complained that he was working blind, a few figures at a time.

The townspeople came up to pose one after another: the mayor, the priest, the gravedigger, Courbet's own mother and sisters. More than forty of them ended up on the canvas. In Ornans, everyone wanted to be in it. That would change once the Paris newspapers arrived.

Before meeting them, notice what is missing. A funeral needs a grave, and Courbet gives it very little room. He also dropped a reminder of what graves are for, right at its edge. It is small and pale against the brown earth.
Something has been dug up with the soil and left beside the grave. Can you spot it?

spots.title: A skull
spots.text: An old skull, turned up by the spade. The cemetery was brand new, so it may be there as a symbol more than a fact: the plain end of every person in the picture.

lesson.text: The grave is cut off by the bottom of the frame. To see it whole, you would have to step forward, which puts you exactly where the last mourner stands. Courbet does not let you watch this funeral from a safe distance. You are attending it.
Courbet took the format of history painting and filled it with ordinary people. The message was blunt: a farmer's burial matters as much as an emperor's.

Now the crowd. Paris critics called these faces ugly, even grotesque, and some suspected Courbet of mocking religion. Judge for yourself. Each of these people was a real neighbor, painted with the red nose or the tired eyes they really had.

lesson.title: Four neighbors
lesson.text: Move through the procession from left to right, the way it walked into the cemetery.

spots.title: The coffin
spots.text: You can hardly see it. The coffin hides under a white cloth marked with black crossed bones, carried by men in wide hats and white scarves. The dead person has no face and no name.

spots.title: The beadles
spots.text: Two church officials in red robes and ribbed red hats. Their flushed faces enraged the critics, who read them as drunkards and the painting as an insult to the Church.

spots.title: The gravedigger
spots.text: Kneeling in shirtsleeves, jacket on the ground, he waits for the priest to finish reading. He is the only one whose day this is simply work.

spots.title: The dog
spots.text: A white hunting dog has wandered in and looks away, toward something outside the picture. Nobody shoos it. Real life does not pause for ceremonies.

lesson.text: The dog is a good guide to everyone else. Follow the human eyes and you find the same thing: the priest reads, a choirboy stares up at a pallbearer, women press handkerchiefs to their faces, men drift. No two people look at the same spot. Grief here is scattered, private, sometimes absent.

The picture could easily have been refused. But a year earlier Courbet had won a medal at the Salon, and medal winners were excused from the selection jury. He used that free pass to hang the largest, least flattering canvas he could.

Earlier painters of funerals arranged their crowds like a pyramid, rising toward a central figure and often toward heaven. Courbet refuses the pyramid. He builds his picture from flat bands, one above the other, like layers of rock.
Three lines hold the whole composition together.

lines.label: The cliffs
lines.text: The limestone cliffs around Ornans draw a hard, level line under a gray sky. No ray of light breaks through, no angel waits above.

lines.label: The row of heads
lines.text: The heads sit at nearly the same height from one end to the other, like a frieze, a long sculpted band on a building. Nobody rises above the rest.

lines.label: The crucifix
lines.text: The only thing that climbs past the cliffs into the sky is the processional cross. It is thin, dark and far from the grave.

lesson.text: So the sky is closed, the crowd is level, and all the weight of that black mass presses down toward the hole at your feet. Many viewers in 1850 felt the picture offered death without consolation. That, as much as the red noses, is what they could not stand.

Two older men near the grave wear knee breeches, long stockings and the kind of coat fashionable around 1793. They are usually identified as veterans of the French Revolution, still dressing like the men they were sixty years before.

Courbet later said that this funeral was really the burial of Romanticism, the art of grand feelings and faraway dreams. After it came the movement he gave a name to, Realism: painting what you can see, in your own time, without improving it.

The canvas stayed unsold all his life. In 1881 his sister Juliette gave it to the French state, and it now fills a wall in the Musée d'Orsay. One question has never been settled. Whose funeral is it? Courbet never said, and the coffin under its white cloth keeps the secret.

quiz.question: Why did the size of the canvas shock people in 1850?
options: It was too small to see the faces
Such a huge format was reserved for heroes, kings and religious scenes
Large paintings were banned from the Salon
quiz.explanation: A canvas nearly seven meters wide was the format of history painting, not of village life.

quiz.question: Who posed for the figures?
quiz.explanation: The mayor, the priest, the gravedigger and Courbet's own family came to his attic studio to pose.

quiz.question: What lies at the edge of the grave?
quiz.explanation: A small pale skull sits on the dug earth, a reminder of where everyone ends.

quiz.question: How did Courbet get the painting into the Salon without facing the jury?
options: He had won a medal the year before, which exempted him
He hung it secretly at night
quiz.explanation: Medal winners were excused from the selection jury, and Courbet used that right.

quiz.question: What is the only element that rises above the line of cliffs into the sky?
quiz.explanation: The thin processional cross is the single vertical that crosses the horizon.

facts.text: Courbet painted the Burial in a vast Paris studio with plenty of room to step back.
facts.explanation: He worked in a cramped attic in Ornans and could not see the whole canvas at once.

facts.text: The mourners in the painting all look toward the coffin.
facts.explanation: No two people look at the same spot, and the dog looks out of the picture altogether.

facts.text: Courbet's sister gave the painting to the French state after his death.
facts.explanation: Juliette Courbet donated it in 1881, and it now hangs in the Musée d'Orsay.
